title: Cyrus
lead: Cyrus II, founder of the Persian empire, who took Babylon in 539 BC. The Bible remembers him as the king who let the exiles of Judah go home and rebuild the temple, and Isaiah calls him the LORD's anointed.

sections.b: Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd and anointed, whom God would grasp by the right hand to subdue nations and rebuild Jerusalem (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1–7). His decree closes Chronicles and opens Ezra (2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–4), and an Aramaic memo of it is quoted in Ezra 6:3–5. Daniel is dated to his reign (Daniel 1:21; Daniel 6:28; Daniel 10:1). Outside the Bible, the Cyrus Cylinder records his claim to have been chosen by Marduk and to have returned peoples and gods to their homes.

sections.h: Cyrus in Isaiah: prophecy or contemporary word?
sections.b: Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 name Cyrus outright. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem, in the 700s BC, named the king some 150 years before his rise. On this view the naming is a deliberate sign of God's lordship over history: "I called you by your name. I gave you a title of honor, though you did not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). Josephus says Cyrus read the prophecy and was moved to fulfill it (Antiquities 11.5–7). Conservative commentators such as John Oswalt defend the unity of Isaiah on these grounds. Most critical scholars assign Isaiah 40–55 to an anonymous prophet writing among the exiles about 545–539 BC, when Cyrus was already conquering. On that view the prophet interprets Cyrus' rise as the LORD's work and the coming fall of Babylon as near, as Joseph Blenkinsopp argues. Both sides agree that the poems present a foreign king as the LORD's "anointed," a title otherwise used of Israel's kings and priests.

Ezra gives Cyrus' decree twice: in Hebrew, as a proclamation inviting the exiles to go up and build (Ezra 1:2–4, repeated in 2 Chronicles 36:23), and in Aramaic, as an archive memo setting the temple's size and paying its costs from the royal treasury (Ezra 6:3–5). Many historians, following Elias Bickerman's classic study (1946), accept both as genuine in substance: the Aramaic memo reads like an administrative record, and the Hebrew proclamation like a herald's announcement in the language of its hearers. The Cyrus Cylinder shows the same policy of restoring shrines and peoples, in Babylonian terms. Other scholars think the Hebrew decree, with its confession of "the LORD, the God of the heavens," has been shaped or composed by Jewish writers, and point out that the Cylinder mentions only Mesopotamian cities. Amélie Kuhrt argued that the Cylinder is royal propaganda in a traditional Babylonian form rather than a statement of a new policy of tolerance.
